About this map

Every one of Toronto’s 158 neighbourhoods is scored on the gap between how much it depends on transit and how well transit actually serves it.

The three scores

  • Need — how transit-dependent a neighbourhood is. We average three things, each ranked from 0 to 1 across the city: the share of residents with low income, the share of commuters who get to work without a car, and how densely people live. Higher means more dependent on transit.
  • Access — how well transit serves it. We combine how many stops sit in the neighbourhood per square kilometre with how often vehicles come through in the weekday morning peak (7–9 am), plus partial credit for busy subway and LRT stations just outside the edge. Higher means better served.
  • Equity gap — need minus access. A large positive gap (pink) is a neighbourhood that leans on transit but doesn’t get much of it. A negative gap (blue) means service runs ahead of need.

Choices worth knowing about

The 2021 Census doesn’t publish two of the numbers we wanted, so we used the closest available stand-ins:

  • There is no “low-income households” figure, so we use the standard Low-income Measure (LIM-AT) — the share of people who fall below it.
  • The 2021 Census dropped the vehicle-ownership question, so we use the share of commuters who travel by something other than a car — walking, cycling, transit — as a stand-in for not having a vehicle.

Not all transit is equal. A subway train carries far more people than a bus, so counting stops alone would flatter a neighbourhood served by a single bus route. Each scheduled trip is weighted by vehicle capacity — roughly bus 1×, streetcar 2.5×, LRT 6×, subway 15× — before frequencies are added up.

Stations don’t stop at the boundary line. A subway station just outside a neighbourhood still serves the people near it, so every neighbourhood gets partial “walkshed” credit for rapid-transit stations within 500 m of its edge — full credit at the boundary, fading to zero at 500 m, about a six-minute walk.

A known limitation

The transit schedule lists the Bloor-Yonge interchange as two separate stations — “Bloor Station” and “Yonge Station”, about 100 m apart — and we don’t merge them. Neighbourhoods around that interchange may show slightly more walkshed credit than they strictly should.

Data snapshot

Built from City of Toronto open data retrieved 1 September 2026; the TTC schedule feed is valid 6 September to 31 October 2026. This is a single point-in-time snapshot — it is not updated as routes, schedules or demographics change.
